content: The kingdom Monera was one of the five biological kingdoms in the traditional system of classification. It included organisms characterized by a prokaryotic cell structure, meaning they lacked a defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Due to this defining feature, the kingdom was also referred to as Prokaryota or Prokaryotae. Before the establishment of Monera as a distinct kingdom, these organisms were classified under two separate divisions of plants: Schizomycetes, which included bacteria and were considered fungi, and Cyanophyta, which were regarded as blue-green algae. However, it is now understood that Cyanophyta are a group of bacteria, commonly referred to as cyanobacteria, and they are not closely related to plants, fungi, or animals. Advances in DNA and RNA sequencing have revealed that prokaryotes can be divided into two major groups: Bacteria and Archaea. These two groups are not more closely related to each other than they are to eukaryotes, which has led to the abandonment of the Monera kingdom. Instead, the classification system has evolved into a six-kingdom model and a three-domain system, where Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya are treated as separate domains or kingdoms. Historically, organisms were initially classified into three categories: animal, vegetable, or mineral, as outlined in Systema Naturae. After the invention of the microscope, attempts were made to fit microscopic organisms into either the plant or animal kingdoms. In 1866, Ernst Haeckel proposed a three-kingdom system, introducing Protista as a new kingdom to include most microscopic organisms. Within Protista, he identified a subgroup called Moneres, which included known bacterial groups such as Vibrio. Haeckel's Protista kingdom also encompassed eukaryotic organisms that are now classified as protists. Over time, it became evident that the Protista kingdom was too diverse to be considered a single kingdom. In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed a five-kingdom system, which placed most single-celled organisms into either the prokaryotic Monera or the eukaryotic Protista. The other three kingdoms in Whittaker's system were the eukaryotic Fungi, Animalia, and Plantae. Further advancements in molecular phylogeny led Carl Woese to propose dividing prokaryotes (monerans) into two distinct groups: Bacteria and Archaea. In his 1990 phylogenetic model, these groups, along with Eukarya, were rooted in a universal common ancestor. This model remains the most widely accepted framework for understanding the evolutionary relationships among life forms. The modern interpretation of these three domains is based on the Universal and Eukaryote Phylogenetic Tree, which relies on 16S rDNA analysis, as presented in the Tree of Life Web Project. Bacteria (Eubacteria) and Archaea (Archaebacteria) differ significantly in the environments they inhabit. Eubacteria include the majority of bacteria that humans encounter, such as Escherichia coli and species of the genus Salmonella. These bacteria are commonly found in and around humans. In contrast, Archaebacteria thrive in extreme environments, such as acidic hot springs and deep subsurface locations beneath Arctic ice. These groups were later renamed Bacteria and Archaea, respectively. However, this renaming has caused some confusion, as the term bacteria in common usage originally referred to all prokaryotic microorganisms, which were previously classified under Monera.
